la:verb:pronuntio.html:
prō-nuntĭo (prōnunc-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
, to make publicly known, to publish, proclaim, announce (cf.: edico, promulgo).
Lit.
In gen.: palam

de sellā ac tribunali pronuntiat, sese ejus nomen recepturum, : cum consules amplius de consilii sententiā pronuntiavissent,: sententiam,to deliver the verdict,: judex ita pronuntiavit,pronounced the decision,: re auditā, pronuntiare,: leges,: signum,: proelium in posterum diem,: iter,; ; : rem in venundando,to notify at the time of sale,: jusserunt pronuntiare, ut, etc.,; cf.: pronuntiare jusserunt, ne quis ab loco discederet,: rerum omnium maximus judex, cujus est non argumentari sed pronuntiare verum,.—Of a public crier: pronuntiare victorum nomina,; .—

In partic.
To nominate, appoint as public officer: aliquem praetorem,; .—
To sentence (post-class.); with inf.: protectores pronuntiati vertere solum in exilio,; cf.: ad bestias,; .—
To promise, proclaim, offer as a reward: praemia militi,; : pecuniam,: tribunis vocatis nummos,; : militibus donativum,: beneficia,: munus populo,: quippe Darius mille talenta interfectori Alexandri daturum pronuntiari jusserat,.—Absol.: pronuntiasse (sc. nummos),.—
Transf.
To speak any thing in public, to recite, rehearse, declaim, deliver, pronounce, etc.: versus multos uno spiritu pronuntiare,; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.—
Esp., to act, perform on the stage: intente instanterque,: actores pronuntiare dicuntur, Müll.: Lucceia mima centum annis in scenā pronuntiavit,.—
To tell, announce, relate, narrate, report: cum eam rem scisset et non pronuntiasset,: mercatores quibus ex regionibus veniant, pronuntiare cogunt,: quae gesta sunt pronuntiare,: aliquid sincere,: alius jam capta castra pronuntiat,.—
To utter, pronounce (cf.: appello, dico): neque tamen ad particula accentu acuto pronuntiatur, § 2: Castorem mediă syllabă productă,; : verba corrupte,.—Hence, prōnuntĭātum (prōnunc-), i, n. In logic, a proposition, axiom; a translation of the Gr. ἀξίωμα, ; cf. .

la:adj:pronus.html:
prōnus, a, um (archaic form of
fem. pronis, Varr. ap. ), adj. [like Gr. πρᾶνής = πρηνής, from root pra-, πρό; cf. prae).
Lit., turned forward, bent or inclined, leaning or hanging forward, stooping, bending down (class.; opp. supinus; cf. cernuus).
Of living beings: puerum imponere equo pronum in ventrem,: pronus pendens in verbera,leaning forward to strike,: ipsum Pronum sterne solo,: pronus magister Volvitur in caput,: pecora, quae natura prona finxit,; .—Poet., of those running swiftly, : leporem pronum catulo sectare sagaci,flying swiftly,.—
Of things, bending forward or downward, going or inclined downward: ilex paulum modo prona, dein flexa,: prona ac fastigiata tigna,: pronae atque vergentes ampullae,: demissus inde pronusque pulvinus,: (urbs) prona in paludes,sinking down,: crateres,overturned,: motus corporis,: cubitus,: prona via,steep,: amnis,: rivi,: currus,. —Absol.: nihil habent proni et supera semper petunt,: per pronum ire,downwards,: per prona voluti,.—
In partic.
Of the heavenly bodies, of time, etc., setting, sinking, declining (poet.): pronus Orion,: sidera,: Titan,: dies,: menses (=celeriter praetereuntes),: anni,.—
Of localities, turned, looking, or lying towards (postAug.).
With dat.: loca Aquiloni prona,: aedificii solum pronius orienti,situated more to the east,.—
With ad: campo patente et ad solem prono,.—
Trop., inclined, disposed, prone to any thing (class.); usu. constr. with ad, in aliquid, or dat.;poet. also with gen.
In gen.
With ad: rei publicae genus inclinatum et quasi pronum ad perniciosissimum statum,: anxitudo prona ad luctum, (from ): boves ad domandum proni,: pronus ad omne nefas,: pronus ad cujusque necem,: ad poëticam,: ad simultates,.—Sup.: ad indulgentias pronissimus, Capit. Anton. 10, 8.—
With in and acc.: in obsequium plus aequo pronus,: in libidines,: saeculum in omnia mala,.—Prov.: prona est timori semper in pejus fides,. —
With dat.: pronus deterioribus,fin.—Comp.: aures offensioni proniores,—
With gen. (poet.): ruendi In ferrum mens prona viris,.—Comp.: unus audendi pronior,.—
In partic.
Inclined to favor, favorable to any thing (post-Aug.).
With dat.: si modo prona bonis invicti Caesaris assint Numina,.—Comp.: cohors Cn. Dolabellae pronior,.—
With in and acc.: prona in eum aula Neronis,.—Comp.: ut quis misericordiā in Germanicum pronior,: in verum nepotem,.—
Absol.: prona sententia,: pronis auribus accipere aliquid,; .— Comp.: quos pronior fortuna comitatur,.—
Easy, without difficulty (mostly post - Aug.): omnia virtuti suae prona esse,: omnia prona victoribus,: pronum ad honores iter,: via ad regnum,: pronum est, it is easy: agere memoratu digna pronum erat,: invitos praebere deos,: facile et pronum est agere,.—Comp.: id pronius ad fidem est,is easier to believe,.—Hence, adv.: prōnē, downwards, pronely (post-class.).
Lit., .—
Trop., readily, willingly; comp. pronius, .

la:adj:pronubus.html:
prōnŭbus, a, um, adj.
pro-nubo
,
of or belonging to marriage, bridal, promoting marriage: canes,pimps,: anulus,wedding-ring,: nox,the bridal night,: flamma,a bridal torch,: dextra,.—Hence, as subst.
prōnŭbus, i, m., = παράνυμφος, auspex (2. b.), the promoter of a marriage, a groomsman, : accepit maritum suum de amicis ejus et pronubis,.—
prōnŭ-ba, ae, f., a woman who attended to the necessary arrangements of a wedding on the part of the bride, a bridewoman (corresp. to the auspex on the part of the bridegroom), Varr ap. ; Müll., Paul. ex ib.; ; ; .—Hence, Pronuba, an epithet of Juno, the patron goddess of marriage, ; .—Transf., of Bellona, as the presider over a marriage in which the bride is obtained by war, ; also, of one of the Furies, ; ; .

prōnuntĭātĭo (prōnunc-), ōnis, f.
id.

A public declaration, publication, proclamation: quā pronuntiatione factā,—Of the decision of a judge, ; ; .— Of the proclamation of a public crier, .—
Expression, speech: cujus opera Graeca pronuntiatione strategemata dicuntur,: certum est, quod ex ipsā pronuntiatione apparet,.—
In partic.
In rhet., delivery, action, manner, ; : bona,; et saep.; ; ; .—
In logic, a proposition: quid est, cur non omnis pronuntiatio aut vera aut falsa sit?.—
Transf., a single articulate sound: elementa proprie dicuntur ipsae pronuntiationes, P.
